content: 0 of 2 minutes, 20 seconds Volume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard Shortcuts Play/Pause SPACE Increase Volume ↑ Decrease Volume ↓ Seek Forward → Seek Backward ← Captions On/Off c Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreen f Mute/Unmute m Decrease Caption Size - Increase Caption Size + or = Seek % 0-9 Live 00:01 02:18 02:20 Pennsylvania reports fourth death linked to measles 02:20 Get more news on Sept. 23, 2026, 10:02 PM UTC By Erika Edwards The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention acknowledged Wednesday that one measles death has occurred so far in 2026 but provided no clarity about who died or where. The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month. On Wednesday, the CDC’s measles outbreak page was updated to show one death with a note that the number “is subject to change” and that the agency will “update its reporting as additional information becomes available.” The change left more questions than answers. The CDC declined to provide details about which death it was referring to or whether it occurred in Pennsylvania. The agency said its National Center for Health Statistics had verified that the death now posted on the CDC website had occurred and that measles had been listed as an underlying cause of death. Two of the people whose deaths health officials reported in Pennsylvania were babies, including a newborn whose mother had measles while she was pregnant. One was a 40-year-old woman who had a history of asthma and severe lung disease, and another was an 18-year-old who developed a rare neurological condition that causes inflammation in the brain and spinal cord. A Pennsylvania Health Department spokesperson said the department did not know which death the CDC was citing. Pennsylvania’s Health Department considers a death to be “measles associated” if the person died within 30 days of showing symptoms and testing positive for the virus. It can also take into account people’s medical records and whether they were exposed to measles before they died. The CDC’s website says it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to “develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles.” As of Wednesday, the CDC had confirmed 3,471 measles cases in 45 states and Washington, D.C., this year. More than 300 people have been hospitalized because of measles infection. Three people died of measles in 2025: an adult in New Mexico and two young girls in Texas. The CDC readily acknowledged those deaths at the time based on information from state health departments. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Health Department reported that its measles case count has soared to 835, with 111 cases in the last seven days. Two-thirds of those cases are in adults, and 164 people have been hospitalized in the state. Nearly all people who have been diagnosed with measles are unvaccinated. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are typically given around ages 1 and 5 and offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life. During measles outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old can receive booster doses

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Quick takes: Typhus outbreak in LA, measles exposure at Philly airport, Legionnaires’ in Chicago News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Measles Legionella Typhoid Share Copied to clipboard The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health is investigating a localized outbreak of flea-borne typhus in the Wilshire Center neighborhood of Los Angeles, the department said yesterday in a press release. Rates of the disease have increased in the city in recent years, with a total of 220 cases documented last year, a record high. The current outbreak includes seven symptomatic case-patients, six of whom were hospitalized. So far this year the county has tracked 109 cases. “As flea-borne typhus cases continue to increase across Los Angeles County, preventing exposure to fleas on free roaming animals and wildlife is more important than ever,” said Muntu Davis, MD, MPH, Los Angeles County Health Officer. “Community members can help protect themselves and their neighbors by keeping pets on flea control year-round, rodent proofing their homes and making sure wildlife cannot live in or around their homes. Simple steps can prevent serious illness.” Last week there were two possible measles exposures at Philadelphia International Airport. The exposures come on the heels of a reported exposure last week at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and highlight high virus activity in the state with the nation’s largest measles outbreak. Today the state will likely top 800 cases, with roughly 100 new cases reported each week, and four measles-associated deaths reported this year. The Hilton Garden Inn North Shore/Evanston, near Chicago, has been linked to two recent Legionnaires’ disease cases in visitors who reported using the hotel’s hot tub and pool during their stay. The case-patients stayed at the hotel in August, and the hotels pools and hot tubs have been closed since early September. “The Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) conducted water sampling and an environmental investigation of the hotel on September 8, 2026,” Evanston city officials said in a statement. “Both confirmed cases reported being in the pool and hot tub areas in August 2026, and those areas have been closed since September 2, 2026.” Water samples from other areas of the hotel did not detect Legionella bacteria, the statement said. Measles outbreak in Chicago shelter cost nearly $9 million, CDC estimates News brief Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Measles Federal Register / Flickr cc In JAMA Network Open yesterday, scientists from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Illinois public health agencies estimated the cost of a 2024 measles outbreak in two Chicago shelters for unhoused people newly arrived in the country at $8.7 million. The economic evaluation tallied the costs of the outbreak, which took place from March 7 to April 30, in terms of the public-health response, direct medical expenses, and productivity losses in patients in isolation or quarantine and those caring for children who missed school or daycare due to isolation. “Measles outbreak responses are highly intensive, requiring rapid case identification and isolation and contact management,” the authors wrote. Cost per infection approached $153,000 In total, 57 people, including 30 women (median age, 3 years) contracted measles amid the outbreak, and authorities traced 3,569 contacts (median age, 17 years). The estimated societal cost was $8.7 million, or $152,636 per measles case. Public-health response costs totaled $1.8 million in personnel costs, $1.4 million in vaccination expenses, $200,489 for lab testing costs, $104,263 for transportation, and $63,023 in other material costs. Though the outbreak placed a considerable cost burden on both public health and health care systems, rapid disease identification and mass vaccination among shelter residents prevented a more costly and larger outbreak. Direct medical costs tallied $4.4 million, mostly from hospitalizations, and estimated productivity losses were $683,895, with 17,113 lost school days. Total health-sector and payer costs, including public health response and direct medical costs, were $8 million ($140,638 per case, and $2,246 per shelter contact). “This outbreak response was one of the most expensive in the measles postelimination era due to the large costs associated with vaccination and isolation and quarantine in hospitals,” the authors wrote. “Though the outbreak placed a considerable cost burden on both public health and health care systems, rapid disease identification and mass vaccination among shelter residents prevented a more costly and larger outbreak.” “Strategies to reduce disease transmission and costs during outbreaks among undervaccinated populations living in congregate settings may include funding non–health care isolation and quarantine spaces and vaccinating new shelter residents on arrival,” the researchers concluded. Ebola outbreak in DR Congo approaches 7,800 cases News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Ebola Viral Hemorrhagic Fever UNMEER / Flickr cc The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to infect those in Ituri province at an alarming rate, according to a new report published by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) yesterday. According to the report, the DRC has 7,773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 deaths, with 40 new confirmed cases and 27 deaths reported during a 48-hour period earlier this week. “Ituri province remains the most affected, with 5,966 cases, including 2,737 deaths, reported from 28 of 36 health zones,” the ECDC wrote. “In total, 84.5% of identified case contacts are under follow-up in the affected provinces.” Without a high rate of case contact follow-up, the outbreak will continue to ravage the region, experts have warned, with new, unknown transmission chains accounting for new cases. Efforts to ensure safe burials Today the World Health Organization (WHO) published an account of a family’s resistance to safe burial techniques in the DRC, with the family refusing a safe and dignified burial for more than 24 hours because they did not want a body bag used. Experts in risk communication and community engagement were called in, and eventually a safe burial took place. The WHO said acts of community engagement and education are the best tools currently used to stop this outbreak. content: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware 71° Measles Health officials report 43 new measles cases in Pennsylvania; state total now topping 800 Pennsylvania's measles outbreak doesn't seem to be letting up, with 43 new cases reported since Monday. By6abc Digital Staff Wednesday, September 23, 2026 8:14PM Share PHILADELPHIA (WPVI) -- Pennsylvania's measles outbreak doesn't seem to be letting up, with 43 new cases reported since Monday. That makes 140 new cases in the past 10 days. RELATED: Pennsylvania health officials urge early measles vaccinations as outbreak grows The state has now reported 835 measles cases in 39 counties so far this year. There have been 164 total hospitalizations. Health officials have announced four measles-related deaths. Health care providers are seeing a surge of interest in vaccinations, doing twice as many in August as usual and nearly 40,000 in the first three weeks of September. content_title: Measles cases in PA closing in on 800
content: FILE – This undated image made available by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows an electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) By David Mowery | dmowery@readingeagle.com | Reading Eagle PUBLISHED: September 22, 2026 at 10:15 AM EDT | UPDATED: September 22, 2026 at 12:10 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The number of reported measles cases in Pennsylvania is nearing 800, including five in Berks County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported in its latest update Monday that 792 measles cases have been confirmed across 39 counties. The department posts updates three times a week at its dashboard, pa.gov/measles . The department’s update noted the following: • New positive cases since Sept. 18: 25 • Total counties: 39 • Total cumulative cases: 792 • Total hospitalizations: 155 • Total confirmed measles-associated deaths: 4 • Measles cases among vaccinated individuals: 4 (less than 1% of cases) According to the dashboard, Lancaster County remains the leader in cases with 323. Cases in the region: Chester County, 76; Lebanon County, 21; Montgomery County, 3; Lehigh County, 2; and Schuylkill County, 1. State health officials said they have administered more than 4,800 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations at 148 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities since late April when the outbreak began. Overall, state health center staff have administered more than 6,900 MMR vaccine doses this year. The department reported that health care providers have seen an increased interest from people seeking MMR vaccinations. In a typical month, Pennsylvania health care providers administer about 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine. Officials said more than 46,000 MMR vaccines were given in August and more than 25,000 doses have been administered over the first two weeks of September. The department advises that the best protection against measles is to get fully vaccinated. The two-dose MMR vaccine boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97% lifetime protection. Those who have two documented doses of MMR do not need another, the department said. Adults who have only one dose or cannot find their vaccination records should talk with a health care provider or pharmacist about getting vaccinated. Officials said measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious short- and long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling, with nearly 20% of people who contract measles being hospitalized. Death from measles, though rare, occurs in 1 to 3 patients per 1,000 cases, they said. Measles is spread when someone who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area, the department said. Symptoms begin with fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), followed by a rash that starts on the head and spreads downward. Without proper protection or supportive care, measles can be deadly, officials said. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. If you believe you were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms, you are advised to contact your health care provider or call the health department’s hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). content_title: Measles vaccine push urged in Americas after World Cup
content: At a glance Measles cases in the Americas reach highest levels in 22 years Guatemala, Mexico, the US, Peru account for 95 per cent of confirmed cases Outbreaks fuelled by low vaccination coverage, FIFA World Cup travel Countries in Latin America are being urged to strengthen vaccination and surveillance to fight measles as the region records the highest number of cases in more than two decades, disease experts say. Low levels of vaccination coupled with travel during the FIFA World Cup have fuelled the resurgence of the highly contagious disease, which spreads easily through the air and mostly affects children. Measles is preventable through vaccination but immunisation coverage for the disease in the Americas is below the level needed to protect the population. So far in 2026 the Americas have recorded the highest number of confirmed measles cases in the last 22 years , according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional office of the World Health Organization. Measles leaves no room for complacency. Each outbreak highlights immunity gaps that must be addressed urgently. - Daniel Salas, executive manager of the special programme for comprehensive immunisation, PAHO Between January and August, more than 51,000 cases of the disease were reported , almost triple the number recorded during all of 2025, when 15,152 confirmed cases were reported and the region lost its measles-free status. In an August advisory , PAHO urged countries in the region to strengthen vaccination, epidemiological surveillance and rapid response to measles outbreaks because the public health risk associated with the disease was “very high”. Daniel Salas, executive manager of the special programme for comprehensive immunisation at PAHO, told SciDev.Net : “Measles leaves no room for complacency. Each outbreak highlights immunity gaps that must be addressed urgently.” World Cup fever Case numbers are particularly high in Guatemala, Mexico, the United States, and Peru, which together, account for 95 per cent of all cases registered in the Americas so far this year, according to PAHO . The US has reported 39 new outbreaks so far this year and 3,471 confirmed cases up to mid-September, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ( CDC ) said in an update last week (18 September). Public health experts say the resurgence of the disease is being driven largely by declining vaccination rates, compounded by the high volume of people traveling across the region for the June-July World Cup, held in Mexico, the US, and Canada. Bianca de Oliveira Cata Preta, a professor in the department of public health at the Federal University of Paraná, Brazil, told SciDev.Net : “The combination of these factors is what seems to have favoured the spread of the virus, giving rise to the scenario we have now.” Measles is the most contagious disease affecting humans. It is estimated that one infected person can infect 12 to 18 other people , “The high mobility associated with international travel and mass events are factors that can favour the spread of the virus within and between countries,” Cata Preta added. PAHO says it is closely monitoring the situation in all countries with sustained measles transmission, supporting affected countries to strengthen surveillance, detect and respond quickly to cases, and close gaps in vaccine coverage. Low vaccination cover Of the measles cases registered in the Americas this year, almost three quarters (73 per cent) were people not vaccinated against the measles virus, according to the PAHO report . For most of the remaining cases, information on vaccination status was unknown or unavailable. The report says most countries and territories in the Americas still have suboptimal vaccination coverage of below 95 per cent, which is needed to protect the population against measles. Only 85 per cent of the regional population have received the two required doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine. There are several possible reasons to explain the drop in measles vaccination coverage, from difficulty of access to a growing rejection of vaccinations and lack of awareness of the risks associated with the disease, believes Cata Preta. “It is important to understand the reasons behind the low vaccination rates in each country in order to then think about strategies to combat the low coverage,” she said. Measles is transmitted through the air or by respiratory droplets when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. It can cause high fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis, and a rash. In some cases, it can also lead to complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness, and can be fatal. Herd immunity Renato Kfouri, vice president of the Brazilian Society of Vaccination and a paediatric infectious disease specialist, told SciDev.Net : “Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent the disease and stop its spread. “International health authorities recommend that at least 95 per cent of the population be vaccinated to prevent transmission.” This is the percentage required to achieve so-called “herd immunity”, when a large percentage of the population becomes immune, making it difficult for a disease to spread. Kfouri believes the case of Brazil illustrates the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage rates. The country registered 15 cases of measles in the first 28 weeks of 2026, all of them imported. This is to be expected, according to Kfouri. But he added: “People travel and can return to the country infected, but the important thing is that these cases, even if they generated secondary cases, were controlled before they could cause outbreaks of the disease.” Maintaining high vaccination coverage and active surveillance for the early recognition of imported cases is essential, stresses Kfouri, especially when the epidemiological situation in neighbouring countries deteriorates

content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services PITTSBURGH Measles Add Topic PA measles cases jump again, but virus is still skipping Allegheny Finch Walker USA TODAY NETWORK Sept. 24, 2026, 10:58 a.m. ET Hear this story Pennsylvania has seen a rise in measles cases, with 835 confirmed cases and four deaths as of late September. The vast majority of cases, over 99%, have occurred in individuals who were not fully vaccinated. Lancaster County is the most affected area, though potential exposures have been reported at a Pittsburgh children's hospital. Weeks after Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. bickered about the Keystone State's measles reporting, measles cases throughout Pennsylvania are continuing to multiply as the end of September approaches. Cases across the commonwealth increased by more than 100 over the past week as of Sept. 23, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health's measles dashboard. Lancaster County, where two measles-associated deaths were reported in August, was still seeing the most illness, with 342 confirmed cases of measles as of Sept. 23. While no cases had been reported among Allegheny County residents, other counties in the area were seeing additional cases. Here's what to know. How many measles cases are there in Pennsylvania? There were a total of 835 confirmed cases of measles spread across Pennsylvania as of Sept. 23, with 111 new cases in the past week, according to the state dashboard. Of those cases, more than 99% occurred in people who were not fully vaccinated, with under 1% occurring in people who were fully vaccinated. A total of 164 people had been hospitalized. Does Pittsburgh have any measles cases? Pittsburgh had no confirmed measles cases as of Sept. 23. But patients at UPMC Children's Hospital were exposed to the disease multiple times in August when out-of-county individuals who were infected with the virus visited the hospital, according to the county health department. Exposures took place on Aug. 12 and Aug. 18 when a patient visited the hospital's emergency department, with additional exposures occurring on Aug. 27. On Aug. 27, multiple groups at UPMC Children's were exposed to the virus, officials said, including those in the Giraffe/Hippo Waiting Room on the third floor from 1 to 4 p.m.; the Giraffe Clinic on the third floor from 2 to 5 p.m.; the cafeteria on the 3rd floor from 3 to 5 p.m.; the main lobby on the first floor from 1 to 5 p.m.; and the Grape/Purple Elevators from 1 to 5 p.m. Here's a look at measles cases in the broader Pittsburgh area as of Sept. 23, the last day the state's measles dashboard was updated: Allegheny: 0 Armstrong: 2 Beaver: 0 Butler: 1 (diagnosed on Aug. 25 according to hospital spokesperson; not reported by state dashboard as of Sept. 23) Fayette: 0 Lawrence: 0 Washington: 0 Westmoreland: 2 Where are measles cases spreading in Pennsylvania? There's confirmed community transmission of measles in Centre, Chester, Clearfield, Indiana, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mifflin, Snyder, Somerset, Union and York counties, according to the state department of health. How many measles deaths have there been in 2026? Pennsylvania's department of health had confirmed four measles-associated deaths across the commonwealth as of Sept. 23. Two of the individuals lived in Lancaster County, one resided in Jefferson County and the fourth was from Mifflin County, according to health department officials. The first two deaths, both infants, according to NPR, were confirmed by the state on Aug. 25. The state confirmed two more deaths on Sept. 15. The third and fourth deaths involved a 40-year-old woman with an active infection and an 18-year-old with a rare neurological complication from measles, NPR reported. None of the individuls were vaccinated. Before 2026, there had been no measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania in about 35 years, according to health department officials. How does measles spread? How contagious is it? Measles spreads through the air when a sick person breathes, coughs or sneezes, according to the Centers for Disease Control. It can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after a person who is sick with the virus leaves the area. It's extremely contagious and can sicken up to nine out of 10 people who come into close contact with an infected person if they aren't protected against the virus. Unvaccinated people are most at risk of catching the disease. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine provides about 97% immunity from measles, according to the CDC. Young children typically don't get their second dose until they reach four to six years of age, leaving them with about 93% protection against the disease. Infants generally don't get their first dose until they're 12 to 15 months old. The CDC notes that infants between the ages of six and 11 months can get a dose of the vaccine if they're going to travel outside of the U.S., though they should still get two additional doses at the recommended ages to provide long-term protection. What are the symptoms of measles? Measles symptoms generally appear within seven to 14 days after coming into contact with the virus, according to the CDC, though the incubation period can last up to 21 days. Symptoms can include a high fever, cough, runny nose, red/watery eyes, white spots inside the mouth and a rash that begins on the face at the hairline and moves downward on the body. The virus can also cause numerous complications, including ear infections, diarrhea, lasting immune system damage, hospitalization, pneumonia, encephalitis, pregnancy problems and death. People who believe they were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Allegheny County residents who are worried about possible exposures should call Allegheny County Health Department at 412-687-2243. Residents throughout Pennsylvania who are concerned about potential exposures should call the Pennsylvania Department of Health’s toll-free hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH. Pennsylvanians can access the measles dashboard, current guidance and additional information at pa.gov/measles. Finch Walker is the Pittsburgh Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network. content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTHCARE Measles Add Topic Measles spread south in Ohio as new cases keep growing Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Sept. 24, 2026, 2:51 p.m. ET Hear this story Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with 196 cases reported across 16 counties this year. The vast majority of measles cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, a surge experts attribute to declining vaccination rates. A new county is reporting measles cases as Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. The state had 16 new cases in the past week, a 66% decrease from the 47 new cases the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 196 cases in 16 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Sept. 24. That's up from 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17; 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10; 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3; 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27; 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20; 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13; and 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Morrow County, northeast of Columbus, joins the list with eight cases reported in the past week. And in Southwest Ohio, two people who tested positive for measles may have exposed others at Cincinnati Children's Hospital's emergency department on Sept. 14 and 15, according to the Cincinnati Health Department. ODH does not show measles cases in Hamilton County as of Sept. 24. "These patients were exposed to measles in the state in which they live and have since been discharged from Cincinnati Children’s and returned to their home state," a Sept. 17 statement from the health department said.The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Sept. 11 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 3,387 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula: 32 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 44 (six new cases) Harrison: 11 Holmes: 9 Knox: 5 Meigs: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 8 (eight new cases) Ottawa: 1 Portage: 1 Trumbull: 8 (one new case) Tuscarawas: 13 Wayne: 44 (one new case) The case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least four people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 23, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Where are measles cases spreading in Ohio? Portage County confirmed its first measles case, the county Health District announced Sept. 8. At the time, no public exposure locations associated with this case had been identified. Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, but the state dashboard shows additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reported 34 new measles cases last week, nearly four times its nine cases the week prior. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

content: Skip to content Press shift + ◄ to open this menu Support Our Work News & Features Outdoors Sports Arts Opinion Events Daily Roundup Newsletters Glacier Park Prints Flathead Living Glacier Journal Sponsored Police Blotter Reader Poll Photos & Video Recent Publications Public Notices Podcasts About Us Advertise Contact Us Search in https://flatheadbeacon.com/ Healthcare Health Officials Identify Three Measles Exposure Sites in Flathead County Exposures occurred Sept. 8-11 at Glacier Highland in West Glacier, Logan Health Primary Care in Columbia Falls and on an eastbound Amtrak train from West Glacier By Zoë Buhrmaster September 21, 2026 The Flathead City-County Health Department on March 11, 2021. Hunter D’Antuono | Flathead Beacon A person infected with measles visited Flathead County from Sept. 8 to Sept. 11, exposing people at three known sites across the valley, health officials announced Sunday. Officials said they are awaiting test results on a suspected case and said more exposure sites may be identified. The Flathead City-County Health Department confirmed two measles cases in residents last year, when Montana saw its first measles outbreak in 35 years. The county has expanded resources for people with questions about the disease, including an online self-assessment tool and a prerecorded measles information phone line. Known exposure sites and dates include: Glacier Highland Gift Store & Restaurant in West Glacier, Sept. 8 to 11 Logan Health Primary Care in Columbia Falls, Sept. 8 between noon and 5 p.m. Amtrak Train 8, eastbound from West Glacier on Sept. 11 Anyone who may have been exposed during those timeframes should monitor for symptoms for 21 days and complete the county’s online self-assessment form, which can be found here. When an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks, they release tiny droplets containing the measles virus. The virus can linger in the air up for to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. It can also spread when a person touches contaminated surface and then touches their mouth, eyes or nose. Initial symptoms usually include a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, along with small white spots inside the cheeks. A red rash typically appears on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. Health officials urge anyone who develops symptoms to call their health care provider immediately. People who believe they may have measles should stay home and avoid visitors until they are no longer contagious or measles has been ruled out. People who are immune through vaccination, lab-confirmed immunity or prior infection, as well as those born before 1957, are generally not considered at risk. Officials said about 90% of unvaccinated people who are exposed will become infected. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is about 97% effective after two doses and is the best protection against the disease. Self-assessment tools, the measles phone line and other resources are available on the county’s measles website, where confirmed cases and exposure locations will be posted. zoe@flatheadbeacon.com

Health ‘We’re literally seeing new forms of measles’: Infectious disease doc warns about scary Pennsylvania development By McKenzie Beard Published Sep. 23, 2026, 11:12 a.m. ET 6262 Comments See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak has taken a disturbing turn. The highly contagious disease has ripped through communities across the Keystone State in recent months, sickening hundreds, sending scores to the hospital and claiming four lives. Now, as the virus continues to spread, doctors are seeing it turn up in patients they rarely encountered before — and learning how to treat them in real time. 3 US measles cases in 2026 have already surpassed last year’s total, which was the highest tally in more than 30 years. weerapat1003 – stock.adobe.com Enter: Congenital measles, a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when a mother who is infected around the time of delivery passes the virus onto her baby in the womb or during birth. For much of history, cases like these were rare. Before vaccines, most people were infected with measles during childhood, so women typically had lasting natural immunity by the time they had children of their own. Later, widespread vaccination provided that same protection without requiring people to contract the disease. But measles, once declared eliminated in the US, is making a comeback nationwide as vaccination rates decline and fewer young adults have natural immunity from prior infection. “Because of this, we’re literally seeing new forms of measles,” Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, told The Guardian. “We don’t have a lot of information about what happens with it.” Just last month, a woman with measles in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, delivered a stillborn baby who died from a ruptured spleen in a case the coroner classified as a measles-associated death. The midwife who attended the birth told the mother that the baby’s death was linked to her severe case of measles and lack of vaccination, according to The Atlantic. 3 Women who contract measles during pregnancy can pass the virus onto their newborn in the womb or during delivery. pressmaster – stock.adobe.com Measles during pregnancy can increase the risk of pregnancy loss, premature delivery and low birth weight. Up to 30% of babies whose mothers are infected around the time of delivery may also contract the virus, putting them at risk for serious illness. “Congenital measles typically presents in the newborn with fever and rash within the first 10 days of life, and can occasionally cause severe complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis and even death,” Dr. Manish Trivedi, head of infectious diseases at AtlantiCare, told The Post. The trouble may not end there. Congenital measles also increases the risk of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, a rare and progressive neurological disorder that causes widespread inflammation and scarring in the brain. It is almost always fatal and has no cure. Adding to the concern is that few pediatricians across the country have experience treating newborns infected with the virus. Earlier this month, the American Academy of Pediatrics published an FAQ on congenital measles to help address that knowledge gap, laying out guidance on preventing, diagnosing and treating the infection in newborns whose mothers have measles. And this isn’t just a theoretical concern. “If measles keeps spreading, we’re going to see more pregnant women exposed to the virus,” Trivedi said. As of Sept. 18, 3,471 confirmed measles cases had been reported across the US in 2026, according to the latest federal data, spanning 39 outbreaks. 3 Newborns are at an increased risk for severe disease from a measles infection. andriano_cz – stock.adobe.com With more than three months still left in the year, that has already surpassed 2025’s total of 2,289 confirmed cases — the highest annual tally in more than three decades. But Trivedi stressed that not all pregnant women are in immediate danger. “Pregnant women are considered at higher risk for complications from measles, but those who already have evidence of immunity are generally well protected,” he said. “The greatest concern is for pregnant women who are not immune and become exposed or infected.” Trivedi recommends that pregnant women check their vaccination history or immunity with their health care provider, especially if they’ve been exposed to measles or live in or travel to an area with an outbreak. 62 What do you think? Post a comment. The catch: The MMR vaccine contains a live, weakened version of the measles virus and can’t be given during pregnancy. “Women who are not immune should be vaccinated before pregnancy or after delivery,” Trivedi said. “If a nonimmune pregnant woman is exposed to measles, she should contact her healthcare provider immediately because intravenous immune globulin can be given within six days of exposure to reduce the risk or severity of infection,” he advised. content: Local Sports High School Huddle Scene Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH What to know about measles in NC with Pennsylvania outbreak announced Iris Seaton Asheville Citizen Times Sept. 23, 2026, 12:34 p.m. ET Pennsylvania has confirmed 25 new measles cases, bringing its total to 792 for the year. Nationwide, measles cases have significantly increased, with several states reporting over 100 cases this year. Symptoms of measles include high fever, cough, runny nose, and a characteristic red, blotchy rash. An outbreak of measles has been announced in Pennsylvania, with 25 new positive cases confirmed since Sept. 18. Nationwide, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that measles cases have increased significantly over the past several years, by hundreds of cases in some cases, including those of Pennsylvania and Utah. As previously reported by the Citizen Times, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced Aug. 31 that a case of measles could have spread to residents of Buncombe County via a sick traveler. The Pennsylvania Department of Health continues to provide up-to-date information on measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths on its measles dashboard at pa.gov/measles. Here's what we know about the outbreak so far, plus information on NC's cases and more. Pennsylvania measles outbreak: What we know The Pennsylvania Department of Health announced an outbreak of measles in the state on Sept. 21. The notice confirmed 792 measles cases across 39 counties in the state so far this year, including 25 new positive cases since Sept. 18, 2026. Latest measles exposure in Buncombe County The latest measles news in Buncombe County happened in August due to a sick traveler, with possible exposure locations including: Exxon, 1920 Four Seasons Blvd., Hendersonville, on Aug. 25 from 9:30-11:45 a.m. - Monitor for symptoms until Sept. 15 Holiday Inn Express, 435 Smokey Park Highway, Asheville, on Aug. 26 from 1-10:30 a.m. - Monitor for symptoms until Sept. 16 Is there measles in North Carolina? How many measles cases are there in NC? The N.C. DHHS says 24 measles cases were identified in the state between December 2025 and February 2026. This includes 17 cases in patients under 18 and five in patients over 18. Of these patients, 68% were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. These numbers do not include measles cases reported in travelers to North Carolina. No further measles cases have been reported in the state since February. How many people are vaccinated against measles in North Carolina? According to the CDC, roughly 93.7% of N.C. kindergarteners were vaccinated for the 2025-2026 school year. This is down slightly from 94.2% in the 2024-2025 school year. Which states have the most measles cases? According to CDC data updated Sept. 18, states with 100 or more cases of measles recorded in 2026 so far include: Pennsylvania - 745 South Carolina - 670 Utah - 527 Texas - 192 Virginia - 178 Wisconsin - 158 Florida - 147 Ohio - 124 Arizona - 110 What are the symptoms of measles? What does a measles rash look like? Symptoms of measles usually begin 7-14 days after exposure, but can appear up to 21 days later. Measles symptoms may include: High fever, potentially exceeding 104 degrees Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Tiny white spots on the inner cheeks, gums, and roof of the mouth appear two to three days after symptoms begin A rash that is red, raised, and blotchy, usually starting on the face and spreading to the trunk, arms, and legs, three to five days after symptoms begin Can measles be deadly? Harvard Health explains that complications of measles are most common among children under the age of five, adults over the age of 20, pregnant women, and people with impaired immune systems. Measles is fatal in up to three out of 1,000 cases. In 2025, the CDC reported that three people died in the U.S. of measles among the 1,912 cases reported. How does measles spread? The state health department website states that the measles virus lives in the nose and throat. It spreads when someone with measles talks, sneezes, or coughs, releasing tiny droplets containing the virus into the air. Droplets can remain airborne and contaminate surfaces for up to two hours. County; officials not alarmed St. Louis Public Radio | By Sarah Fentem Published Sept. 23, 2026 at 5:00 a.m. CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Chuck Gomez / Amtrak Three cases of measles in Missouri are tied to an Amtrak train trip to Chicago. A person with measles who visited several public spaces in the St. Louis region earlier this month is connected to an Amtrak train trip associated with other cases, public health officials confirmed. The Franklin County resident is the third confirmed case of measles tied to the train journey. A person infected with measles on Aug. 27 boarded the train in Sedalia. Later, a St. Louis County resident, who was vaccinated, tested positive for the virus. On Monday, the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services released a list of places the infected person from Franklin County visited during the weekend of Sept. 12, which included several restaurants in St. Louis and St. Louis and Franklin counties in addition to a Cardinals game at Busch Stadium. St. Louis County Department of Public Health Director Kanika Cunningham said Tuesday that health officials are not treating the cases as cause for alarm. “There are some pockets of individuals who you know are unvaccinated, but right now we're not seeing this as an outbreak,” she said. “We're monitoring every day.” Franklin County Health Director Tony Buel said that he had so far not heard of the resident spreading the disease to anyone else. “I don’t believe that the person who was in Franklin County at the locations of concern has spread it to anybody,” he said. “[There’s] no confirmation of that anywhere or even any suspected cases. But keep in mind onset can be as long as 21 days.” Missouri has so far logged 10 cases of the highly contagious virus, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after exposure, though they can appear up to 21 days afterward. Early symptoms include fever, runny nose, cough and red or watery eyes, followed by the characteristic measles rash. It’s particularly dangerous for very young or very old people. The United States this year has seen more measles cases than it has in decades. Close to 3,500 people have been confirmed infected so far in 2026, about 1,000 more than in the entirety of 2025. According to the CDC, 13% of children under 5 years old with reported infections have been hospitalized. As measles cases rise around the country, it’s going to be more common to see cases pop up in Missouri and St. Louis, said Nathan Koffarnus, assistant communicable disease chief at the state’s health department. “There is actually more measles circulating in our country than has been common in decades,” he said. “And so it is important to be aware of that and to be concerned.” The infected person was in several situations with prolonged, close contact, Koffarnus said. That means more people may be infected. “Those cars can be pretty full, and people are in close quarters for a prolonged period of time,” he said. “Where the exposure took place is particularly challenging. When we have these, you know, subsequent cases that were also out in the community, visited a lot of places, there's certainly a lot of opportunities for exposure to others at those spots.” Both Cunningham and Koffarnus said the best protection is the two-shot measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination, which is 97% effective. Even if people who are vaccinated get a “breakthrough” case, they said, it’s likely to be less severe than an unvaccinated person would experience. The measles vaccine, for the most part, does not wane in power. A person who receives the full series of shots likely does not need to worry about getting a booster or another dose. “I think right now the messaging is we need to raise awareness,” Cunningham said. “If you were at these places, check your vaccination status. If you're unvaccinated, quarantine, call your doctor, let them know, monitor for symptoms.” Have a question or comment about this story? Email St. Louis Public Radio. Got a news tip? Washington-Watch > Washington Watch CDC, Epidemiologists Work on Definition for Measles Deaths — Standard workgroup process began over the summer by Kristina Fiore, Director of Enterprise & Investigative Reporting, MedPage Today September 22, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday The CDC is indeed working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) on a definition for measles deaths, but the initiative was launched earlier this year and it was not at the request of the CDC. That's according to CSTE spokesperson Amy Heldman, MPH, who explained that a CSTE workgroup was launched earlier this summer "to develop future guidance to inform measles epidemiology case investigations associated with deaths." "The workgroup will work collaboratively with CSTE leadership and CDC to apply CSTE's consensus-building processes to develop a standardized case definition related to measles deaths," Heldman said in an email to MedPage Today. Convening the workgroup was part of an established and longstanding consensus-building process, not something requested by CDC, she added. CSTE hosts a number of workgroups with CDC, and this is standard practice based on the needs of jurisdictions, she said. "Determining how diseases and conditions are monitored and investigated and how data are shared at the national level is a rigorous, collaborative process involving CDC, state, tribal, local, and territorial applied epidemiologists, and other partners," Heldman said. "It is CSTE's role to convene applied epidemiologists in states and territories to reach consensus and develop guidance, criteria, and resources for public health surveillance activities." Working on a new definition for measles deaths raised eyebrows because of the way it was announced. Earlier this month, CDC Director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, JD, altered public reporting of measles deathsopens in a new tab or window on the CDC website at the request of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The CDC's website initially listed the two measles-associated deaths recorded by Pennsylvania, but Kennedy asked Schwartz to remove them. In place of the number appeared an asterisk, which remains on the site todayopens in a new tab or window. That asterisk section includes a note that CDC is working with CSTE to "develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles." The section also says that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) "does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause" -- which confused expertsopens in a new tab or window because NCHS is not intended for outbreak data. Instead, the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System has historically been used to track outbreaks by collecting state data. "Typically, the CDC goes with whatever the state reports," said one CDC source familiar with the process who did not want to be named. "It's almost like the CDC wants to make it more difficult to count confirmed deaths," the source said. "I suppose Kennedy wants the definition to be as restrictive as possible so that it appears practically no one is dying from measles." Pennsylvania currently reports four measles-associated deathsopens in a new tab or window. It reported 97 cases in the past 7 days, and a total of 792 cases in 2026, making it one of the hardest-hit states during a measles resurgence that began in 2025. Other states that have been hit particularly hardopens in a new tab or window include Texas, South Carolina, and Utah. Last year, Texas had three measles-associated deaths. content: Search | RU | EN | KG | Home News Local newsEconomyIncidentsExclusiveHealthSportsEcology About Kyrgyzstan Weather Advertising on the Website Weather Home News Local newsEconomyIncidentsExclusiveHealthSportsEcology About Kyrgyzstan For Tourists Home » News » Local news » In Bishkek, they discuss how to prevent new outbreaks of measles in Central Asia In Bishkek, they discuss how to prevent new outbreaks of measles in Central Asia Евгения Комарова • 25.09.2026, 13:13 • Local news Подробнее Переводчик с русского Аналитика событий Люди и общество Read on Telegram Read on Facebook In Bishkek, a subregional strategic dialogue titled "Immunization in Central Asia: from outbreak response to sustainable protection" has begun. Within the framework of the event, representatives from Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan are discussing ways to increase vaccination coverage and the need to transition from merely responding to outbreaks of infections to their prevention. Also participating in the discussion are representatives from UNICEF and the European Regional Office of the World Health Organization. The dialogue is organized by the Ministry of Health of Kyrgyzstan in collaboration with the UNICEF Country Office in the country and the UNICEF Centre of Excellence. Deputy Minister of Health Gulbara Ishenapysova emphasized that high population mobility, labor migration, and active trade and transport links create common risks for the spread of infectious diseases in the region. She noted that "high and sustainable vaccination coverage is not only a national task but also a common challenge for our subregion." According to the deputy minister, recent cases of measles underline the importance of timely identification of gaps in immunization to prevent new outbreaks. During the meeting, participants are addressing issues of sustainable financing for immunization programs, digitization of processes, improving data quality, epidemiological surveillance, introduction of new vaccines, and cooperation between countries. Kyrgyzstan plans to share its experience in the digitization of the immunization system and the development of information systems, while other countries in the region will present practices for using data to improve policy and epidemiological surveillance. UNICEF representative in Kyrgyzstan Samman Tapa noted that long-term investments in training healthcare workers, cold chain logistics, and information systems are essential for protecting children. Particular attention is being paid to the issues of insufficient vaccination coverage and identifying populations that have not been vaccinated. As a result of the dialogue, participants plan to outline further steps for financing immunization programs, data sharing, and strengthening cooperation in Central Asia. Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Chicago/ Crime & Emergencies Chicago Measles Alerts Spread From Union Station To Chinatown Hotel By Jo Marquez Published on September 25, 2026 SpringHill Suites Chicago Chinatown — Additional Measles Exposure Location Google Street View Chicago's measles scare just got bigger. Along with warning commuters about three separate exposure windows at Union Station, city health officials have listed a Chinatown hotel among the places where a person with a confirmed case of the highly contagious virus may have exposed others. The Chicago Department of Public Health flagged the SpringHill Suites at 2357 S. Wentworth Ave. as a public exposure site tied to a domestic traveler who was there from 10:45 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 12 through 3:40 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 13, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. The department also warned, in a notice first reported by CBS Chicago, that commuters passing through Union Station at 255 S. Canal St. may have been exposed on three separate occasions: between 10:25 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. on Sept. 10, between 8:45 p.m. and midnight on Sept. 12, and between 1:40 p.m. and 9 p.m. on Sept. 13. The hotel exposure window overlaps with some of the Union Station windows. Union Station also appeared on an exposure list earlier this year — one potential exposure was reported there after 8 p.m. on Aug. 27 and on Aug. 28, per the same CBS Chicago report. Why a Two-Hour-Old Room Can Still Be Dangerous Measles is notoriously persistent in the air. According to guidance on measles from the Chicago Department of Public Health measles facts page, the virus can remain airborne and infectious in an enclosed space for up to two hours after an infected person has left, and up to 90% of non-immune people who are exposed will go on to contract it. That combination of lingering infectiousness and near-total transmission risk among the unvaccinated is why health officials move quickly whenever a confirmed case surfaces in a high-traffic public space. Union Station itself is about as high-traffic as it gets. The terminal serves more than 3 million Amtrak passengers and 35 million Metra commuter rail riders annually across more than 300 trains a day, according to Chicago Union Station. That volume means even a narrow exposure window, like the 7-hour-20-minute Sunday afternoon alert, could theoretically have put thousands of travelers at risk. Anyone who was in either location during the listed windows should watch for measles symptoms, which the CBS Chicago report notes include rash, high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. Those symptoms can take seven to 21 days to appear after exposure, and health officials say anyone who develops them should call ahead before showing up at a doctor's office or emergency room, rather than walking in and risking further spread. The MMR vaccine is available at no cost to all Chicago residents, including through CDPH immunization clinics. Illinois Cases Already Outpace All of Last Year The exposure warnings land amid a broader statewide surge. The Illinois Department of Public Health reported 22 confirmed measles cases statewide in 2026 as of Sept. 22 — already more than the 14 total cases recorded in all of 2025, though still well below the 67 cases seen in 2024. Illinois' first 2026 case was confirmed Feb. 17 in Metro East following out-of-state travel, while Chicago logged its first case of the year on June 23 in an international traveler, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. Nationally, the picture is starker still. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 3,471 confirmed measles cases and 39 outbreaks across the United States as of Sept. 17, compared with 2,289 total confirmed cases in all of 2025. The surge has been fueled in part by interconnected regional travel; a confirmed case in late August involved a passenger aboard Chicago-bound Amtrak Train 318, which prompted exposure warnings across both Missouri and Illinois transit channels, according to the St. Louis County Department of Public Health. Hoodline previously reported on St. Louis County's first case in two decades. Illinois still maintains a statewide school measles vaccination rate of 96.78%, per the Illinois Public Health Association. Chicago-Crime & Emergencies Crime & Emergencies in ... Ongoing outbreaks in Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas, and Utah have documented hundreds of cases, mostly among unvaccinated people. And while local and federal politicians debate the definitions and impact of those measles-associated deaths, health experts worry that we’re overlooking the real problem: the threat of a full-scale epidemic. Today, we talk to one of those experts – epidemiologist Michael Mina – to figure out who’s most at risk and whether there’s any way for us to turn this epidemic around. Photograph: Hannah Beier/Reuters Analysis Why the CDC is excluding measles deaths in Pennsylvania even as outbreak appears to be ‘accelerating’ Melody Schreiber Centers for Disease Control and Prevention refuses to count four measles deaths in the state though doctors are ‘seeing new forms’ of disease The US Centers of Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its measles dashboard on Friday – but it’s still not counting four measles deaths in Pennsylvania, where the outbreak appears to be accelerating and cases are appearing in ways providers have never seen before. Members of Congress on Monday requested an “immediate briefing” on the decision to change how measles deaths are reported as cases continue to rise throughout the United States, reaching levels not seen in decades. A possible measles exposure was reported in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia last week. The delay in death reporting is “curious” even after the CDC switched how it counts deaths, said Debra Houry, former CDC chief medical officer. It takes one to two days for the CDC to receive updated data to the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) after states finish death investigations. “Pennsylvania concluded the investigation on the first two deaths, so CDC would have these records by now,” Houry said. Pennsylvania asks CDC for emergency help as measles outbreak spreads Read more Meanwhile, the outbreak “seems to be accelerating”, said Dr John Goldman, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. “And we’re seeing, actually, types of measles we’ve never seen before,” he added. Doctors are now treating congenital measles – newborns who contracted the virus in utero or at birth – which was once exceedingly rare because most pregnant people were protected by vaccines or, before immunization, surviving measles in childhood. “Because of this, we’re literally seeing new forms of measles,” Goldman said. “We don’t have a lot of information about what happens with it.” Pennsylvania has reported 731 cases, but that number is likely an undercount, he said. Frequently when patients come to the hospital with measles, they mention that others at home are sick as well – but they haven’t been tested, Goldman said. On average, one to three people for every 1,000 cases will die of measles, and one in five will be hospitalized. The current deaths and hospital admissions in Pennsylvania are “definitely not proportional to what would be expected”, Houry said, and she believes the official numbers are “very much an undercount”. Under-testing can make it challenging to do contact tracing and sick people may not realize they need to isolate – both of which can make the spread of measles more likely. Providers are preparing for more cases and more deaths. “It’s not rocket science. If we see more measles, we’ll see more deaths,” Goldman said. “I suspect that we’re not going to see a break until most people in most communities are immune either by vaccine or infection.” Typically, the CDC collects data from states, including causes of death. Death certificates are issued at the state or local level; there are no federal death certificates. But now, the agency is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to define deaths from measles. While the CDC has its own measles case definition, it has relied upon the World Health Organization’s definition of measles deaths. Until a measles death definition is created, the CDC is relying on NCHS data, which “identifies measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). She did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about why the death count was still delayed, or whether all deaths would receive a CDC definition. Before this outbreak, measles deaths were rare in America; there were none for a decade. “When there aren’t deaths, you don’t need a precise definition,” Houry said. Pennsylvania developed a definition, and the CDC could consider adopting it, she said. Erica Schwartz, the CDC director, denied in an interview that deaths were being miscounted for political reasons, pointing instead to the process of creating a definition. “If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have Covid, often that was called a Covid-related death,” Schwartz said, referencing misinformation about how Covid deaths were counted. In reality, Covid deaths were likely under-counted. Pennsylvania’s definition of “measles death” clearly excludes unrelated deaths, so the bus scenario would not apply, Houry said. “Dr Schwartz’s comments are not only not helpful, but contribute to misinformation.” But this isn’t the most important issue right now, she added. “I would focus less on the definition itself and responding to the measles outbreak, and that’s what the focus of the CDC director should be.” Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, has cast doubt on the Pennsylvania deaths and reportedly instructed Schwartz not to include them in the CDC tally. Kennedy only mentioned the measles outbreak once in a speech spanning nearly an hour and a half at an anti-vaccine conference on Thursday. He noted only that deaths from measles are headline news and he asked that severe side effects and deaths from vaccines get the same attention. About one to two people in a million experience severe side effects from vaccines, while with measles one in five people are hospitalized and one to three in 1,000 die. Pennsylvania has responded aggressively to the outbreak, standing up more than 100 pop-up clinics and requesting additional vaccination support from the CDC. The state department of health has “done a spectacular job of dealing with this”, Goldman said. Tests have a 24-hour turnaround time. “I have called them up on a Thursday before the holiday weekend and arranged for them to do testing before it closed at noon the following day,” Goldman said. “They have provided us with information, and they have provided us with really really good support.” While there is a likely undercount of cases, “it’s not because they couldn’t get a test”, he said. “It’s because they were sick at home and did not seek medical care.” The response hasn’t been limited to the health department, Houry noted. “Health systems and clinicians are really stepping up across the state to get vaccines to their communities.” Before this outbreak, Goldman was the rare American doctor who had seen measles, once in 1988 and once in 1992. Between 1992 and 2026, he didn’t see a single case. Now, “we’re seeing at least one every day”, he said. He’s preparing for three to six more months of this. “Never in my life did I think I was ever going to see measles again,” he said. He fears for other vaccine-preventable diseases: whooping cough, diphtheria, polio. “In a way, I think this is a warning,” he said. “What worries me is measles is conceivably the canary in the coal mine.” Explore more on these topics Pennsylvania US healthcare MMR Vaccines and immunisation Trump administration Health US politics analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Partner of woman killed by US hunter who allegedly mistook her for deer says death ‘no accident’ Why a supercharged El Niño is putting Hawaii in the bullseye of more storms ‘I’m 100% natural’: how Japan’s 90-year-old bodybuilder is still winning titles In latest blow to Obamacare, Trump is threatening the entire US health system Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters Most viewed Most viewed

(KY3) -The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed more than 3,000 measles cases nationwide so far this year, including 10 in Missouri. “Here recently we have seen an increase in measles cases in the state of Missouri,” said Stephanie Woehl of the Springfield-Greene County Health Department. Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases known. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services published a health alert earlier this month warning residents of surging measles cases in the Midwest. The department notified the St. Louis area Monday about a third measles exposure, linked to a Chicago-bound train on Aug. 27. “We are seeing a resurgence of the measles virus because individuals who are receiving the MMR vaccine are declining,” Woehl said. Missouri’s measles vaccination rate stands at 89.5%, far below the 95% coverage level health officials recommend to prevent community outbreaks and achieve herd immunity. “The measles vaccine is very effective. It’s a two-dose series, if you get both doses in the series, 97 percent effectiveness, with one dose, 93,” Woehl said. Health experts say measles can be difficult to diagnose early because symptoms resemble a common cold. The red-brown rash associated with measles appears in later stages of infection. Woehl recommends residents take proactive steps to protect themselves. “Check your evidence of immunity now, check your vaccination records, talk to your healthcare provider. If you do not have evidence of receiving the MMR vaccine, now is a great time to get that vaccine,” Woehl said. Health officials also recommend that anyone experiencing symptoms call ahead before visiting a clinic. This allows staff to prepare and prevent exposing others in waiting rooms and public spaces. following Scottsdale pharmacy exposure Close Maricopa County has reached the highest count of measles recorded in the area in three decades. By Alaina Kwan Published: Sep. 21, 2026 at 4:16 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google PHOENIX (AZFamily) — Maricopa County health officials last week confirmed another case of measles, bringing the county’s total to 28 cases this year — the highest count recorded in the area in three decades. The Maricopa County Department of Public Health on Thursday announced the latest exposure risk stems from a Walgreens near Via Linda and Frank Lloyd Wright Boulevard in Scottsdale. Officials said an infected individual visited the pharmacy earlier this month. Public health officials advise anyone who visited the store during that window to monitor for symptoms through Sept. 29. Measles symptoms typically include a high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes, followed by a distinct rash. Local medical experts warn that the virus spreads rapidly and poses serious health risks, particularly as children return to classrooms and respiratory virus season begins. “It can linger in a room for hours, even after you leave, up to two hours,” said Dr. Frank LoVecchio, a local emergency physician. “So if I have measles and I walk into a room and I cough and it’s in the air, I leave the room and two hours later... someone else walks in the room, they can catch measles.” LoVecchio noted that declining vaccination rates over recent years have made communities more vulnerable to outbreaks. Because the virus is airborne and highly contagious, an infected person can easily spread it to 10 or 12 unvaccinated individuals in a shared space. While most children recover from the illness, health officials emphasize that measles can lead to severe complications if transmitted to higher-risk populations. “Most kids who get measles are not going to die from it,” LoVecchio said. “The problem is when they give it to older people, and when they bring it home and bring it to somebody maybe who’s not vaccinated, that older person could develop pneumonia, could develop meningitis or a brain infection. And, you know, unfortunately, they could die of that.” Physicians stress that widespread immunization remains the most effective way to halt community spread and protect vulnerable populations, including infants and immunocompromised individuals who cannot receive the vaccine. “The good news is we can prevent it, usually with vaccination, but we all need to do it,” LoVecchio said. “The great majority of it needs to be vaccinated to kind of protect everyone. If your child’s vaccinated, they’re less likely to bring it home.” The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is typically administered to children as a two-dose series, while adults without documented immunity generally require a single dose. According to LoVecchio, protective antibodies can begin developing as early as one week after the first dose. Residents seeking vaccination or those who believe they may have been exposed should contact their primary care provider before visiting a clinic or emergency department in person. (KATU) — Clark County Public Health is investigating two confirmed measles cases involving unvaccinated children, including a possible exposure at a Battle Ground school. One person who tested positive for measles was at River HomeLink, 610A SW Eaton Blvd., while contagious, health officials said. The possible exposure occurred Thursday, Sept. 17, from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Public Health is working with Battle Ground Public Schools to identify students and staff who are not protected against measles. Those people will be excluded from school, child care and other public settings for 21 days, officials said. People who have received two doses of the measles vaccine are well protected, according to Clark County Public Health. The agency said two doses are about 97% effective at preventing the disease.
