content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Local Weather WE INVESTIGATE Video Newsletters Sunny 74o Watch 24/7 Trending Nick Bosa Restaurant break-ins 🎸 Dolly Parton Day ⛽ Gas prices 🛩️ Fleet Week 🎙️ Women Who Lead 🗳️ Election guide Expand Centers for Disease Control and Prevention CDC reports first measles death amid confusion over Pennsylvania cases The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month. By Erika Edwards | NBC News • Published September 23, 2026 • Updated on September 23, 2026 at 5:10 pm Getty Images Computer illustration of a measles virus particle. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention acknowledged Wednesday that one measles death has occurred so far in 2026 but provided no clarity about who died or where. The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month. On Wednesday, the CDC’s measles outbreak page was updated to show one death with a note that the number “is subject to change” and that the agency will “update its reporting as additional information becomes available.” Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are WATCH HERE The change left more questions than answers. The CDC declined to provide details about which death it was referring to or whether it occurred in Pennsylvania. The agency said its National Center for Health Statistics had verified that the death now posted on the CDC website had occurred and that measles had been listed as an underlying cause of death. Two of the people whose deaths health officials reported in Pennsylvania were babies, including a newborn whose mother had measles while she was pregnant. One was a 40-year-old woman who had a history of asthma and severe lung disease, and another was an 18-year-old who developed a rare neurological condition that causes inflammation in the brain and spinal cord. A Pennsylvania Health Department spokesperson said the department did not know which death the CDC was citing. Health Sep 15 Pennsylvania teen dies from measles complications, health officials report Health Sep 13 Pennsylvania woman dies from measles complications, marking the state's third this year Health Aug 25 Two die of measles in Pennsylvania outbreak Pennsylvania’s Health Department considers a death to be “measles associated” if the person died within 30 days of showing symptoms and testing positive for the virus. It can also take into account people’s medical records and whether they were exposed to measles before they died. The CDC’s website says it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to “develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles.” As of Wednesday, the CDC had confirmed 3,471 measles cases in 45 states and Washington, D.C., this year. More than 300 people have been hospitalized because of measles infection. Three people died of measles in 2025: an adult in New Mexico and two young girls in Texas. The CDC readily acknowledged those deaths at the time based on information from state health departments. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Health Department reported that its measles case count has soared to 835, with 111 cases in the last seven days. Two-thirds of those cases are in adults, and 164 people have been hospitalized in the state. Nearly all people who have been diagnosed with measles are unvaccinated. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are typically given around ages 1 and 5 and offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life. During measles outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old can receive booster doses. 9:33 Governor Shapiro speaks after first 2 Pa. residents in 35 years die of measles Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro touted the effectiveness of the MMR vaccine to combat measles after the first two unvaccinated residents of the state in 35 years were confirmed to have died of measles. excerpt: An infected traveler rode six Amtrak routes through California including San Joaquin County and the Stockton station, prompting a statewide measles exposure alert.

content_title: Measles alert issued after infected passenger travels through Stockton station
content: California health officials are warning travelers about a potential measles exposure after an unvaccinated passenger infected with the virus passed through multiple counties aboard Amtrak trains and connecting buses earlier this month — including San Joaquin County and the Stockton station. The California Department of Public Health said the traveler moved through Los Angeles, Kern, San Joaquin, Butte, Sacramento and Alameda counties before continuing on to Colorado. San Joaquin County officials are urging anyone who may have shared transportation with the passenger or visited the same stations to monitor for symptoms, especially if they are unvaccinated, immunocompromised, pregnant or caring for young children. The traveler arrived in Los Angeles from Chicago on Sept. 12, then traveled through Bakersfield, Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento and Emeryville before departing California for Denver. Health officials identified several Amtrak train and bus routes where exposures may have occurred: Train #5717: Los Angeles to Bakersfield, Sept. 12 Train #717: Bakersfield to Stockton, Sept. 12 Train #3717: Stockton to Oroville, Sept. 12 Train #3718: Oroville to Sacramento, Sept. 13 Train #749: Sacramento to Emeryville, Sept. 13 Train #6: Emeryville to Denver, departing Sept. 14 Officials also said exposure may have occurred at stations and transit centers along those routes. Anyone who rode those trains or was present in the stations during those times should watch for symptoms for up to 21 days after possible exposure. California has reported 59 measles cases across 13 counties as of Sept. 14, according to state health officials. Nearly all cases involved people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. The latest exposure alert comes amid a nationwide measles resurgence. Public health experts have linked many recent outbreaks to declining vaccination rates and international travel. Because measles is among the most contagious diseases known, a single infected person can spread the virus to as many as nine out of 10 unvaccinated people they encounter. Health officials continue to say that the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine remains the most effective protection against the disease. Two doses provide long-lasting immunity for most people. Dr. Rita Nguyen, California's assistant state public health officer, said the exposure serves as another reminder of the importance of vaccination, particularly for young children and people with weakened immune systems. "Measles is one of the most contagious infections that can lead to severe life-long consequences including permanent brain damage and can also be fatal, especially for children," Dr. Nguyen said. Symptoms typically develop seven to 21 days after exposure and may include: An unexplained rash that spreads across the body Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or even breathes. The virus can remain suspended in the air and linger in a room for up to an hour after the infected person leaves. UC Davis pediatric infectious disease specialist Dr. Dean Blumberg noted that direct contact is not required for transmission, making measles especially difficult to contain among unvaccinated populations. Monitor for fever, rash, or other symptoms for 21 days after exposure. Contact your health care provider if you are unvaccinated or unsure of your vaccination status. Call ahead before visiting a doctor's office, urgent care clinic or hospital if you develop symptoms. Review your vaccination records and discuss MMR vaccination with your provider if needed. People who have received the recommended two doses of the MMR vaccine are generally considered protected and face a significantly lower risk of infection. For most vaccinated Californians, the risk remains low. But health officials say the exposure highlights how quickly measles can spread through public transportation hubs and other crowded settings. Travelers who may have been exposed should watch for symptoms and confirm that they and their family members are up to date on vaccinations. Louis-area bars, health officials warn St. Louis Public Radio | By Rob Edwards Published Sept. 21, 2026 at 5:34 p.m. CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Measles is a highly contagious virus. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, if one person is infected, up to 9 out of 10 people nearby will also be infected if they are not protected. Health officials are warning of possible measles exposures this month at Busch Stadium and several bars and businesses in the St. Louis area. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services said Monday that people may have been exposed to measles at several locations between Sept. 12 and Sept. 14. The most prominent was at Busch Stadium, where someone with measles was present between 6 p.m. and 11:30 p.m. Sept. 12. Health officials said the person was seated in Section 141. That same day, possible exposures were reported at the Cat’s Meow in Soulard from 3:30 p.m. to 7:50 p.m. and Paddy O’s downtown from 9:30 p.m. until closing. The other locations were in Pacific and Chesterfield: Little Ireland in Pacific from 11:30 a.m. until an unknown time Sept. 13. B&H Market in Pacific from 6:30 p.m. Sept. 13 until an unknown time. Pacific Brew Haus from 8 p.m. until closing Sept. 13. Goodcents in Chesterfield from 3 p.m. until 5:15 p.m. Sept. 14. Bud’s Market in Pacific from 5:30 p.m. to 7:45 p.m. Sept. 14. The health department is asking people who were at those locations during the listed times to monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days from the time they were first exposed. The warning comes just days after St. Louis County health officials confirmed the first measles case in a county resident in two decades. The person, who was fully vaccinated, had ridden an Amtrak train to Chicago on Aug. 27. Measles is highly contagious and spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after exposure, though they can appear up to 21 days afterward. Early symptoms include fever, runny nose cough and red or watery eyes, followed by the characteristic measles rash. Have a question or comment about this story? Email St. Louis Public Radio. content: South Jersey Sports Varsity Living Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH NJ thus far not impacted by neighboring Pennsylvania measles outbreak Risha Inaganti Cherry Hill Courier-Post Sept. 22, 2026, 4:47 a.m. ET Measles cases are on the rise throughout the country, with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reporting 3,471 confirmed cases in 2026 as of Sept. 17. Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus that spreads through the air. Cases in 2026 have spread across 47 states and U.S. jurisdictions, including New Jersey. So far this year, New Jersey has only had one confirmed case of measles in 2026. That case came in April from a Hudson County resident. Although the Garden State has remained safe from the ongoing outbreak, its neighbor right over the Delaware River is struggling, as Pennsylvania has seen 792 cases and four measles-associated deaths this year. These deaths were the first measles-related fatals for Pennsylvania in 35 years. Pennsylvania has seen measles cases in 38 counties and exposures all across the state. A handful of exposures have occurred in Philadelphia. According to the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), exposures took place at four CHOP Philadelphia hospital areas Sept. 11. There was also a potential exposure at Philadelphia International Airport on Sept. 13. Those traveling in the airport from Sept. 13 at 7:25 p.m. to Sept. 14 at 12:05 a.m. have been potentially exposed, according to officials. Affected areas include terminals B and F, as well as common areas that connect to terminals C, D and E. Despite reaching close to the state border, the New Jersey Department of Health has confirmed that there are no active exposure locations in the state at this time. The department said that measles can be best prevented with the MMR vaccine, which stands for measles, mumps and rubella. State officials are asking all residents to stay up to date on MMR vaccines, especially before travel. Those traveling internationally with an infant should talk to a pediatrician about receiving the vaccine early. Updated: 10:19 PM EDT Sep 22, 2026 Editorial Standards i Maegan Summers Reporter PEACH BOTTOM, Pa. — A pop-up vaccination clinic at the Robert Fulton Fire Company in Peach Bottom, Pennsylvania, brought members of the local Plain community together on Tuesday to receive measles vaccinations as the state works to combat a growing outbreak. Hearst Owned WGAL Peach Bottom families seek protection from measles As of Tuesday, Pennsylvania has 792 measles cases, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Advertisement Many families from the Plain community call Peach Bottom home. When WGAL visited the clinic Tuesday afternoon, we saw multiple vans and buggies bringing people of all ages to the site. Some attendees, who spoke off camera, said they came to get vaccinated because they were scared of getting sick. They explained that many people in the Plain community have contracted measles, and they wanted to protect themselves and their children. Hearst Owned WGAL Pop-up clinics expand vaccine access The Pennsylvania Department of Health, which hosted the clinic, said it is one of many pop-up vaccine clinics being held in areas with high case numbers. For privacy reasons, filming inside the clinic was not allowed. "Measles virus is among the most infectious viruses we have. It doesn't ask what your race is, what your religion is, or where you live," said Dr. Robert Bonacci, medical advisor to the secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Health. "Our outreach isn't to target a particular community. It's really focused on where the measles virus is spreading in Pennsylvania." The department emphasized that these pop-up clinics aim to make vaccines more accessible. Dr. Bonacci said, in August, the Department of Health and its providers vaccinated more than 46,000 people with the MMR vaccine. He said that, typically, they vaccinate 25,000 people in a month. Hearst Owned WGAL "These clinics help us provide information for folks, provide a forum for them to ask questions about the vaccine and to educate them about what's going on with the outbreak and with the measles," Bonacci said. "We're making it easy for folks to get vaccinated against measles, because we know here in Pennsylvania, the way that we're going to end this outbreak is by getting as many people vaccinated and fully protected against measles as we can." The health department reiterated that people who are fully vaccinated are 97% protected against measles. Officials also said they plan to hold additional pop-up vaccine clinics at partnering locations in the future. content: Latest U.S. Iran War Cuba Plans World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Face the Nation | Full Episodes Transcripts About Us Watch CBS News Face The Nation Cassidy says Trump needs to be "radically honest" on vaccines amid measles outbreak By Kaia Hubbard Kaia Hubbard Politics Reporter Kaia Hubbard is a politics reporter for CBS News Digital, based in Washington, D.C. Read Full Bio Kaia Hubbard Updated on: September 20, 2026 / 3:37 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Washington — GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana on Sunday urged the president to be "radically honest" when he's speaking about vaccines, as the U.S. this year has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades. "I would just ask the president to be aware that people are listening to him — if he discourages immunization, there'll be fewer people immunized, and if we're speaking of measles, there'll be more people sick in the hospital or even die," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." The Trump administration has been encouraging parents to vaccinate their children against measles in recent months, as cases have climbed. But Mr. Trump has cast doubt on the vaccine and its schedule, including through an executive order last month suggesting that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, should be given as three separate shots. He also claimed without evidence that the MMR vaccine, if not separated, could be "lethal." Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, the president said he is going to "demand" that drug companies split up kids' vaccines into five doses, given in six-month intervals. He said, "the vaccine size will be much, much less" and argued that it will lead "to a massive reduction in autism." "So instead of having a massive dose of 82 or 88 different vaccines pumped into your arm, we'll take out certain vaccines that people are a little worried about," Mr. Trump said. Cassidy, a medical doctor, said he didn't know which vaccines the president was referencing. But he stressed that there needs to be "radical honesty." "Have the president come forward — what is he basing this on? Who's giving him advice?" Cassidy said. Cassidy said he approaches the issue "as a physician," saying people are worried, and "we need to address that worry where it is." "If you want to be radically honest, the vaccines are safe, they've been proven to be safe, and the current regimen has been timed to be most convenient to the parent," he said. "At any point, the parent can say, 'I want something different.'" Cassidy urged the president to explain his position, asking, "Why do you think this vaccine is lethal?" "Have you ever seen a case of lethality?" he said. "And what about the people who are not vaccinated, who are getting sick and even dying?" The Louisiana Republican cited recent measles-related deaths, including a 40-year-old and an 18-year-old. He said, "having measles is not a kind of victimless kind of experience," comparing it to drunk driving. "You can drink and get drunk, but if you drive, you're going to hurt other people," Cassidy said. "You can get measles, but when you start spreading it to other people, a 40-year-old dies, an 18-year-old dies, children in a neonatal intensive care unit are at risk. People have got to realize, and the government has to realize it. The president should be saying, 'Be vaccinated. It is safe and effective.'" He added, "We should have a common voice of radical honesty, of trying to help the American people understand what is safe. And if the president calls it lethal, then where are you getting your information, Mr. President? And if you really don't have it, why are you willing to risk the lives of fellow Americans?" The Louisiana Republican, who's leaving office early next year after the president endorsed his GOP challenger, chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Asked what he needs to hear from the nominee for FDA commissioner, Heidi Overton, at her hearing this week, Cassidy said, "I need to hear that she understands that calling the measles vaccine lethal is absurd, and we need radical honesty." Cassidy also noted that the president's nominee for surgeon general, Nicole Saphier, said in a committee hearing last week that the MMR vaccine is not lethal, while encouraging people to get vaccinated. Cassidy said she earned his vote. "When somebody is willing to be honest to the American people and say that vaccines are safe, you should be taking it, and the consequence of not can even include death, well, what else can you ask for when it comes to vaccines?" he said. opened in Edwardsville in May 2026. Health officials have confirmed a case of measles in Edwardsville. The Madison County Health Department said people who were at Salt + Smoke at 410 N. Main St. in Edwardsville between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. Sept. 10 may have been exposed to measles. Anyone who was at that location during that time should monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days after the potential exposure, according to the health department. Symptoms of measles can include fever, cough, runny nose and the characteristic red rash that starts around the head or face and spreads to the rest of the body. People who were potentially exposed and develop symptoms should contact their medical provider. Health officials say they should call in advance before arriving so medical facilities can take precautions to prevent additional exposures. Missouri health officials notified the public on Monday about another case of measles in the St. Louis region. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services said people may have been exposed to measles at several locations between Sept. 12 and Sept. 14. The most prominent place was Busch Stadium, where someone with measles was present between 6 p.m. and 11:30 p.m. Sept. 12. Health officials said the infected person also visited several bars and businesses in St. Louis, Chesterfield and Pacific. Have a question or comment about this story? Email St. Louis Public Radio. content: California officials warn of possible measles exposure in 6 counties due to infected Amtrak rider Watch: California officials warn of possible measles expo... California officials warn of possible measles exposure in 6 counties due to infected Amtrak rider KCRA / KQCA US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 2:57 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 8:45 PM PDT Sep 21, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jeremiah Martinez Digital Producer Denzen Cortez Reporter California officials warn of possible measles exposure in 6 counties due to infected Amtrak rider Updated: 8:45 PM PDT Sep 21, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jeremiah Martinez Digital Producer Denzen Cortez Reporter State public health officials are warning about a possible measles exposure across multiple California counties after an infected passenger traveled across the country on trains and buses. The California Department of Public Health said the unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state using Amtrak trains and thruway buses with transfers in at least six counties: Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Joaquin. Advertisement Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. People who are not vaccinated, particularly young children and pregnant people, face the highest risk of severe illness and even death, according to officials. The passenger arrived in California from an Amtrak train to Los Angeles on Sept. 10, according to officials. After arriving in Los Angeles, they took a route to Bakersfield and then went to Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento, and Emeryville before leaving the state to Denver. Here is the route the passenger took: Sept. 10: Departed Chicago at 1:30 p.m. Sept. 12: Arrived at Los Angeles Union Station on Sept. 12 at 8:12 a.m. Sept. 12: Departed Los Angles at 10:55 a.m. and arrived at Bakersfield station at 1;45 p.m. Sept. 12: Departed Bakersfield at 2:02 p.m. and arrived at Stockton—San Joaquin St Station at 6:29 p.m. Sept. 12: Departed Stockton at 6:35 p.m. and arrived at Oroville bus/thruway stop at 9:30 p.m. Sept. 13: Departed Oroville at 4 p.m. and arrived to Sacramento Valley Station at 6:05 p.m. Sept. 13: Departed Sacramento at 6:53 p.m. and arrived to Emeryville Station at 8:36 p.m. Sept. 14: Departed Emeryville at 8:25 a.m. and arrived to Denver at 6:59 p.m. Officials said people who were passengers on those trains or buses or who were at the stations on those days have been exposed to measles. Officials added it's working with federal partners and local health departments to notify people who may have been exposed. "This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles," Assistant State Public Health Officer Dr. Rita Nguyen said in a statement. "The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and provides long-lasting protection against measles. Vaccination protects both our own families and those who are too young to be fully vaccinated." KCRA 3’s Denzen Cortez spoke with Dr. Dean Blumberg, professor and chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UC Davis Health, who said measles can spread without direct contact with an infected person. “The issue with measles is it's likely the most contagious infection known to humans,” Blumberg said. “You don't even have to be in the same room at the same time with somebody to get measles, since the virus can linger in the air for an hour or two after they left.” Blumberg said vaccination dramatically changes the risk for someone who may have been exposed. “If they've been vaccinated, the good news is that they're protected and they're immune,” Blumberg said. “If they're not vaccinated, then measles has about a 90% attack rate, meaning there's a nine times out of ten chance that somebody is going to get infected.” As of Sept. 14, 2026, a total of 59 measles cases have been reported in 13 counties in California, according to officials. Patients were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status in 94 percent of cases. What to do if you have been exposed or have symptoms Officials said to monitor symptoms, such as watching for a fever and/or unexplained rash from seven to 21 days after exposure. If symptoms develop, officials urged people to call your doctor for guidance. If anyone suspects they have measles, it's recommended to call their health care provider before visiting any health care facility to avoid exposing others. People who are not vaccinated against measles or are unsure of their status are recommended to contact their doctor about receiving the vaccine. Two doses of the vaccine are needed to be fully immunized, officials said. Measles virus. 3D illustration showing structure of measles virus with surface glycoprotein spikes heamagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion protein Dr_Microbe - stock.adobe.com Clark County Public Health is investigating two cases of measles in unvaccinated children. The cases were reported on September 23. People who were at a Battle Ground school may have been exposed. According to the health department, a person who tested positive visited River HomeLink on Southwest Eaton Boulevard on September 17. They were there from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Clark County Public Health is working with Battle Ground Public Schools to identify students and staff who are not protected against measles. Those individuals will be excluded from school, child care and other settings for 21 days. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Anyone who was at the school and has not been vaccinated against measles or has not had measles in the past is at risk for getting sick. The health department recommends staying home and out of public places for three weeks. During that time, anyone who believes they have symptoms of measles should call their health care provider before visiting the medical office to make a plan that avoids exposing others. Griffen Smith Lee Enterprises 2 min read An electron microscope image of a measles virus particle on Feb. 4, 2015. Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Loading Audio Player By Instaread, Please Wait... http://www.bozemandailychronicle.com offers audio versions of articles using Instaread. Some words may be mispronounced. A person infected with measles who visited Flathead County potentially exposed the public at three separate locations from Sept. 8 to Sept. 11, health department officials announced Sunday. Flathead County is asking those exposed at the public locations to monitor their symptoms for 21 days, as measles is a highly contagious viral disease that causes a high fever and a red blotchy skin rash. “We are awaiting test results for a suspected case and anticipate that additional exposure sites may be identified,” health officials said in the announcement. The following locations were confirmed as potential exposure areas for the disease. The exposure period can last up to two hours as measles can stay airborne after an infected person leaves the area. Glacier Highland — Gift Store and Restaurant 12555 Highway 2 E., West Glacier, MT, 59936 Sept. 8-Sept. 11 Logan Health Primary Care 1675 Talbot Road, Columbia Falls, MT, 59912 Sept. 8 from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m. Amtrack Train No. 8 traveling eastbound from West Glacier Sept. 11 The Flathead City-County Health Department asked those who are potentially exposed to complete a measles exposure self-assessment on the department’s website. If someone has symptoms of measles, officials recommend calling a healthcare provider immediately and asked people to stay home until one is no longer contagious or measles are rules out as the illness. The prevalence of measles has increased by more than 1,000 cases nationwide compared to 2025, according to data from John Hopkins University. In Montana, five people in Helena tested positive for measles in March, and one person infected with measles visited Missoula County in November 2025, the Missoulian reported. People immune through vaccination, lab-confirmed immunity or prior infection, or those born before 1957 are generally not considered at risk for infection, the health department said. Meanwhile, those who are unvaccinated from measles have a 90% chance of infection if exposed to the disease. “Measles is a very contagious disease that spreads mainly through the air,” the health department said. “When an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks, tiny droplets containing the virus are released and can remain in the air for up to two hours. This means someone can get measles even without direct contact with the infected person.” Measles usually starts with a fever, cough or runny nose and red eyes. Small white spots can also appear inside the cheeks. About seven to 14 days after exposure, a red rash appears, beginning on the face and then spreading to the rest of the body. The best way to prevent measles is through vaccination, according to the health department. A standards measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is about 97% effective. People interested in vaccination can contact their healthcare provider or schedule an appointment with the heath department online or by calling 406-751-8110. Griffen Smith is the local government reporter for the Missoulian. He is a 2023 graduate of the University of Montana School of Journalism and previously served as the editor of the Seeley Swan Pathfinder. Posted 6:50 PM, Sep 22, 2026 and last updated 7:10 PM, Sep 22, 2026 The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) on Tuesday announced one new confirmed case of measles in the state. The case is in Chippewa County, and at this time, DHS said there are no reports of public exposures associated with it. Since August, DHS said confirmed measles cases have also been reported in Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, Marathon and Vernon counties. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Measles is a highly contagious disease that can be spread from person to person through the air and can stay in the air for two hours after a sick person coughs or sneezes. It can cause serious health complications, including pneumonia, brain damage and deafness, and can sometimes be deadly, according to DHS. If you develop symptoms, DHS advises residents to call a health care provider, even if they are not aware of a specific exposure. Symptoms of measles typically appear 10 to 21 days after exposure to the virus. Let's talk: Hey there! content_title: Potential measles exposure in St. Louis area after third case linked to train ride
content: ST. LOUIS, Mo. — There are now at least three measles cases linked to an exposure on a train in Missouri. The original case was in Jackson County, the second case in St. Louis County and a third person in Franklin County has become infected. The third patient visited several locations around St. Louis between Sept. 12-14. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services (DHSS), along with local health officials, are warning about possible measles exposure at those locations. Below are listed the date, times and locations of where exposure may have been possible: - Sept. 12 between 3:30 p.m. and 7:50 p.m. at The Cat's Meow in Soulard - Sept. 12 between 6 p.m. and 11:30 p.m. at Busch Stadium in section 141 - Sept. 12 between 9:30 p.m. and closing of Paddy O's - Sept. 13 from 11:30 to an unknown time in Little Ireland in Pacific, Mo. - Sept. 13 from 6:30 p.m. to an unknown time at B&H market in Pacific, Mo. - Sept. 13 from 8 p.m. until close at Pacific Brew House in Pacific, Mo. - Sept. 14 from 3 p.m. to 5:15 p.m. a Goodcents in Chesterfield, Mo. - Sept. 14 from 5:30 p.m. until 7:45 p.m. at Bud's Market in Pacific, Mo. The patients are linked to an exposure that happened on a train that left Sedalia on its way to Chicago in August. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that typically begins with fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. One person with measles can easily pass it on to 9 out of 10 people around them who are unvaccinated or do not have natural immunity, the DHSS said in a press release. Symptoms typically appear 7-14 days after contact with the virus. Tiny white spots may appear inside the mouth 2-3 days after symptoms begin. Measles rash appears 3 to 5 days after the first symptoms. It usually begins as flat, red spots that appear on the face at the hairline. They then spread downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs and feet. Exposed individuals should monitor for measles symptoms for 21 days from the date of exposure and contact their local public health agency if symptoms appear. People who think they have measles should isolate themselves and call their health care provider before arriving to be tested. More information about measles and county-level MMR vaccination rates can be found at Health.Mo.Gov/Measles
